0. Introduction¶

Dataset¶

  • Title: AWTAD quadriceps sEMG – barbell back squat.
  • Source: primary data recorded by the AWTAD graduation-project team (not taken from Kaggle or UCI); the raw files are kept in data/raw/ and are not public. Format: one CSV per set, exported from Delsys Trigno.
  • Description: surface EMG from the left and right quadriceps of 33 female participants, recorded with two wireless Delsys Trigno sensors at 2148 Hz while each participant did one or two sets of 5 barbell back squats. Markers in each file split the set into reps: 63 sets and 314 reps in total.
  • Why this dataset: it is the data of our graduation project, AWTAD, which looks for left/right muscle imbalance. This project is a chance to explore it properly before building the final system, and the topic (sports health and injury prevention) matters to us.

Problem definition¶

What the data is about. For each rep we know how strongly each leg's quadriceps worked. A large difference between the legs is a muscle imbalance, which is linked to injury risk and to asymmetric training. We measure it with the Symmetry Index, per rep: $SI = \dfrac{|RMS_L - RMS_R|}{\max(RMS_L, RMS_R)}$, and the rep is an imbalance if SI ≥ 0.15.

Main questions

  1. How common is imbalance, and is it stable for the same person (set 1 vs set 2)?
  2. Which signal features, apart from amplitude, differ between balanced and imbalanced reps?
  3. Which features repeat the same information?
  4. Can a simple model predict SI for a participant it has never seen?

Expected insights. We expected amplitude features to dominate (SI is built from RMS), so the real question is what the frequency, pattern and timing features add. We also expected the imbalance to be a property of the person rather than of a single rep, and the weaker leg's signal to look different (noisier, different frequency content).

Outline: 1 loading · 2 the raw signal · 3 preprocessing · 4 features and cleaning · 5–6 EDA · 7 modeling · 8 dashboard · 9 insights & conclusion · 10 references.

In [1]:
import csv, re, warnings
from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import signal, stats
warnings.filterwarnings('ignore')

DATA_DIR = Path('../data/raw') # folder that holds one sub-folder per participant
FS = 2148.1481                 # Trigno sampling rate (Hz)
SI_THRESHOLD = 0.15

# fixed colours used in every plot
C_L, C_R = '#2a78d6', '#eb6834'        # left / right leg
C_BAL, C_IMB = '#1baf7a', '#6250d6'    # balanced / imbalance
GREY = '#8a8984'
plt.rcParams.update({'figure.dpi': 110, 'axes.spines.top': False, 'axes.spines.right': False,
                     'axes.grid': True, 'grid.color': '#e4e3df', 'grid.linewidth': .6, 'font.size': 9,
                     'axes.titleweight': 'bold'})

1. Loading the data¶

The Trigno files aren't plain CSVs: they start with 7 lines of metadata, and the marker table sits in extra columns to the right of the signal. So we read them with a small parser that pulls out:

  • the left-leg EMG (column 2) and the right-leg EMG (column 4)
  • the marker times
In [2]:
def load_trial(path):
    with open(path, encoding='utf-8-sig', errors='replace') as f:
        rows = list(csv.reader(f, skipinitialspace=True))
    left, right, markers = [], [], []
    for row in rows[8:]:
        if len(row) > 1 and row[1].strip(): left.append(float(row[1]))
        if len(row) > 3 and row[3].strip(): right.append(float(row[3]))
        if len(row) > 8 and row[5].strip() == 'General': markers.append(float(row[8]))
    return dict(left=np.array(left), right=np.array(right), markers=np.array(markers))

data = {}
for path in sorted(DATA_DIR.glob('*/*.csv')):
    trial = int(re.search(r'_(\d)\.csv$', path.name).group(1))
    data[(path.parent.name, trial)] = load_trial(path)

overview = pd.DataFrame([{'subject': s, 'trial': t, 'length_s': len(d['left']) / FS, 'n_reps': len(d['markers']) - 1}
                         for (s, t), d in data.items()])
print(overview.subject.nunique(), 'participants |', len(overview), 'sets |', overview.n_reps.sum(), 'reps')
print('Only one set:', overview.groupby('subject').size().loc[lambda s: s == 1].index.tolist())
print('Sets without 5 reps:', overview[overview.n_reps != 5][['subject', 'trial', 'n_reps']].values.tolist())

33 participants | 63 sets | 314 reps
Only one set: ['Abeer', 'Lulu', 'SaraA']
Sets without 5 reps: [['Khawla', 1, 4]]

Data-quality notes. Abeer, Lulu and SaraA have only one set, and Khawla's first set has 4 reps. We keep them, but it's worth knowing.

2. What the signal looks like¶

Before computing anything we look at the raw signal. We compare a participant with a clear imbalance (Wintana) with a symmetric one (Angie). Dashed lines are the rep boundaries.

In [3]:
def plot_raw(subject, trial):
    d = data[(subject, trial)]
    t = np.arange(len(d['left'])) / FS
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(11, 3.8), sharex=True, sharey=True)
    for ax, side, col in zip(axes, ['left', 'right'], [C_L, C_R]):
        ax.plot(t, d[side][:len(t)], color=col, lw=.4)
        for m in d['markers']: ax.axvline(m, color='#52514e', ls='--', lw=.8)
        ax.set_ylabel(f'{side} (mV)')
    axes[0].set_title(f'{subject} – set {trial}'); axes[1].set_xlabel('time (s)')
    plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

plot_raw('Wintana', 1)
plot_raw('Angie', 1)

Figure 1. Raw EMG of both legs for a participant with a clear imbalance (Wintana, top) and a symmetric one (Angie, bottom). Dashed lines are the rep markers.

Wintana's right leg is clearly more active than her left, while Angie's two legs look alike. That difference is exactly what we want to detect.

Frequency content (PSD)¶

We compute the power spectral density of every recording so the filters are chosen from the data, not from habit.

In [4]:
psd = []
for d in data.values():
    for side in ['left', 'right']:
        f, P = signal.welch(d[side] - d[side].mean(), FS, nperseg=4096)
        psd.append(P / P.sum())
psd = np.array(psd)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 3))
ax.semilogy(f, np.median(psd, axis=0), color=C_L)
ax.axvspan(20, 450, color='#e4e3df', alpha=.6, label='20–450 Hz')
ax.axvline(60, color='#52514e', ls=':', label='60 Hz mains')
ax.set_xlim(0, 600); ax.set_xlabel('frequency (Hz)'); ax.set_ylabel('power'); ax.legend(frameon=False)
ax.set_title('Median PSD – all recordings'); plt.show()

print('Power above 450 Hz (max):', psd[:, f > 450].sum(axis=1).max().round(4))
print('Power below 20 Hz (median / max):', np.median(psd[:, f < 20].sum(axis=1)).round(3), '/', psd[:, f < 20].sum(axis=1).max().round(3))

Power above 450 Hz (max): 0.001
Power below 20 Hz (median / max): 0.009 / 0.177

Figure 2. Median power spectral density of all recordings. It sets the filters: 20–450 Hz band-pass and a 60 Hz notch.

  • Above 450 Hz there is almost no energy: the sensor already low-passes in hardware.
  • Below 20 Hz a few files carry some energy. That's movement artefact (cable and skin motion during the squat).
  • 60 Hz shows a small peak in a few files: mains noise from the building.

Decision: band-pass 20–450 Hz, plus a 60 Hz notch.

3. Preprocessing and rep segmentation¶

  1. Remove the DC offset (the mean). An offset would bias RMS and zero-crossing counts.
  2. Band-pass 20–450 Hz (4th-order Butterworth).
  3. Notch at 60 Hz.
  4. Linear envelope: absolute value, then a 6 Hz low-pass. This gives a smooth curve of how active the muscle is at each moment.

We use filtfilt, which filters forward and backward, so there is no time shift. That matters because we compare the timing of the two legs.

Then each set is cut into reps using the markers.

In [5]:
def preprocess(x):
    x = x - x.mean()
    b, a = signal.butter(4, [20, 450], btype='bandpass', fs=FS)
    x = signal.filtfilt(b, a, x)
    b, a = signal.iirnotch(60, 30, fs=FS)
    return signal.filtfilt(b, a, x)

def envelope(x):
    b, a = signal.butter(4, 6, btype='low', fs=FS)
    return np.clip(signal.filtfilt(b, a, np.abs(x)), 0, None)

def rep_bounds(markers, n):
    idx = np.clip((markers * FS).astype(int), 0, n)
    return [(idx[i], idx[i + 1]) for i in range(len(idx) - 1)]

d = data[('Wintana', 1)]
n = min(len(d['left']), len(d['right']))
t = np.arange(n) / FS
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 3))
for side, col in [('left', C_L), ('right', C_R)]:
    ax.plot(t, envelope(preprocess(d[side][:n])) * 1000, color=col, label=side)
for i, (s, e) in enumerate(rep_bounds(d['markers'], n), 1):
    ax.axvline(s / FS, color='#52514e', ls='--', lw=.8)
    ax.text((s + e) / 2 / FS, ax.get_ylim()[1] * .9, f'rep {i}', ha='center')
ax.set_xlabel('time (s)'); ax.set_ylabel('envelope (µV)'); ax.legend(frameon=False)
ax.set_title('Wintana – envelope per leg, split into reps'); plt.show()

Figure 3. Envelope of each leg for Wintana's first set, split into 5 reps by the markers.

4. Feature extraction¶

For every rep and each leg we compute these groups:

Group Features What they measure Depends on amplitude?
Amplitude RMS, MAV, iEMG, VAR, WL, envelope peak and mean How strongly the muscle is activated yes
Pattern Zero-crossing rate, slope-sign-change rate, Hjorth mobility and complexity How often and how irregularly the signal changes no
Frequency Mean freq (MNF), median freq (MDF), peak freq, spectral entropy Dominant frequencies; linked to fatigue and fibre type no
Timing (fraction of the rep) Onset, time-to-peak, burst duration When the muscle switches on and peaks no
Envelope shape Skewness, kurtosis, coefficient of variation Shape of the activation curve no
Coordination between legs Cross-correlation, correlation, coherence Whether both legs work together in the same pattern no
Fatigue Slope of MDF across the 5 reps Whether frequency drops as the muscle tires no

For every per-leg feature we also compute the left/right difference two ways:

  • _si = |L−R| / max(L,R): the size of the difference, from 0 to 1
  • _diff = L − R: the direction of the difference

Why timing as a fraction? Some participants squat slowly and others fast. A fraction of the rep makes them comparable.

In [6]:
AMPLITUDE = ['rms', 'mav', 'iemg', 'var', 'wl', 'env_peak', 'env_mean']

def leg_features(x, env):
    n, dx = len(x), np.diff(x)
    thr = 0.01 * np.std(x)                      # ignore tiny noise wiggles
    zc = np.sum((x[:-1] * x[1:] < 0) & (np.abs(dx) >= thr))
    ssc = np.sum((dx[:-1] * dx[1:] < 0) & ((np.abs(dx[:-1]) >= thr) | (np.abs(dx[1:]) >= thr)))
    mob = np.sqrt(np.var(dx) / np.var(x))
    comp = np.sqrt(np.var(np.diff(dx)) / np.var(dx)) / mob

    f, P = signal.welch(x, FS, nperseg=min(1024, n))
    keep = (f >= 20) & (f <= 450); f, P = f[keep], P[keep]
    p = P / P.sum()

    peak = np.argmax(env)
    active = env >= 0.5 * env[peak]
    return {
        # amplitude
        'rms': np.sqrt(np.mean(x ** 2)), 'mav': np.mean(np.abs(x)), 'iemg': np.sum(np.abs(x)) / FS,
        'var': np.var(x), 'wl': np.sum(np.abs(dx)), 'env_peak': env[peak], 'env_mean': env.mean(),
        # pattern
        'zc_rate': zc / (n / FS), 'ssc_rate': ssc / (n / FS), 'hjorth_mob': mob, 'hjorth_comp': comp,
        # frequency
        'mnf': (f * P).sum() / P.sum(), 'mdf': f[np.searchsorted(np.cumsum(P), P.sum() / 2)],
        'pkf': f[np.argmax(P)], 'spec_ent': -(p * np.log2(p + 1e-12)).sum() / np.log2(len(p)),
        # timing (fraction of the rep)
        'onset_frac': np.argmax(active) / n, 'ttp_frac': peak / n, 'burst_frac': active.mean(),
        # envelope shape
        'env_skew': stats.skew(env), 'env_kurt': stats.kurtosis(env), 'env_cv': env.std() / env.mean(),
    }

def both_legs(xl, xr, el, er):
    a, b = el - el.mean(), er - er.mean()
    cc = signal.correlate(a, b) / (a.std() * b.std() * len(a))
    lags = signal.correlation_lags(len(a), len(b))
    f, C = signal.coherence(xl, xr, FS, nperseg=min(1024, len(xl)))
    return {'env_xcorr_peak': cc.max(), 'env_xcorr_lag_ms': lags[cc.argmax()] / FS * 1000,
            'env_corr0': np.corrcoef(el, er)[0, 1], 'coherence_20_100': C[(f >= 20) & (f <= 100)].mean()}

def si(l, r):
    return abs(l - r) / max(abs(l), abs(r))

rows = []
for (subject, trial), d in data.items():
    n = min(len(d['left']), len(d['right']))
    xl, xr = preprocess(d['left'][:n]), preprocess(d['right'][:n])
    el, er = envelope(xl), envelope(xr)
    for rep, (s, e) in enumerate(rep_bounds(d['markers'], n), 1):
        fl, fr = leg_features(xl[s:e], el[s:e]), leg_features(xr[s:e], er[s:e])
        row = {'subject': subject, 'trial': trial, 'set_name': f'{subject}_{trial}', 'rep': rep, 'duration_s': (e - s) / FS}
        for k in fl:
            row[k + '_L'], row[k + '_R'] = fl[k], fr[k]
            row[k + '_si'], row[k + '_diff'] = si(fl[k], fr[k]), fl[k] - fr[k]
        row.update(both_legs(xl[s:e], xr[s:e], el[s:e], er[s:e]))
        rows.append(row)

df = pd.DataFrame(rows)
for side in 'LR':   # fatigue: slope of MDF over the reps of each set
    df['mdf_slope_' + side] = df.groupby('set_name')['mdf_' + side].transform(lambda s: np.polyfit(np.arange(len(s)), s, 1)[0])
df['mdf_slope_diff'] = df.mdf_slope_L - df.mdf_slope_R

df['si_rms'] = df['rms_si']
df['label'] = (df.si_rms >= SI_THRESHOLD).astype(int)
df['weak_side'] = np.where(df.rms_L < df.rms_R, 'L', 'R')

META = ['subject', 'trial', 'set_name', 'rep', 'si_rms', 'label', 'weak_side']
FEATURES = [c for c in df.columns if c not in META]
is_amp = lambda c: any(c.startswith(a + '_') for a in AMPLITUDE)
AMP_FEATS = [c for c in FEATURES if is_amp(c)]
NON_AMP = [c for c in FEATURES if not is_amp(c)]
print(df.shape, '| amplitude features:', len(AMP_FEATS), '| other features:', len(NON_AMP))

(314, 99) | amplitude features: 28 | other features: 64

4.2 Cleaning¶

The table has no missing values, no infinite values and no duplicates, so nothing needs to be filled or dropped. The cleaning steps that matter here are:

  • Signal cleaning (section 3): DC removal, 20–450 Hz band-pass and 60 Hz notch.
  • Types: trial, rep and label as integers; subject and weak_side stay as text.
  • Column names: lower case, _L / _R for each leg, _si / _diff for the left/right difference.
  • Outliers: we keep them. With 33 people, an extreme value is usually a real participant (for example SI > 0.5), not an error.

We save the result as app/clean_data.csv, the file the Streamlit dashboard reads.

In [11]:
df[['trial', 'rep', 'label']] = df[['trial', 'rep', 'label']].astype(int)
df.to_csv('../app/clean_data.csv', index=False)
print('Saved clean_data.csv:', df.shape)

Saved clean_data.csv: (314, 99)

Outlier check (IQR rule). We count the reps outside 1.5 × IQR for the label and the strongest features. They are flagged, not removed: they come from real participants, not from recording errors.

In [12]:
check = ['si_rms', 'ssc_rate_si', 'zc_rate_si', 'ssc_rate_diff', 'env_cv_L', 'env_cv_R', 'mnf_diff', 'duration_s']
q1, q3 = df[check].quantile(.25), df[check].quantile(.75)
outside = (df[check] < q1 - 1.5 * (q3 - q1)) | (df[check] > q3 + 1.5 * (q3 - q1))
pd.DataFrame({'outlier reps': outside.sum(), 'share': outside.mean().round(3),
              'participants': [df.subject[outside[c]].nunique() for c in check]})

Figure 5. Histogram of SI over all reps (left) and bar plot of mean SI per participant (right). Dashed line = 0.15 threshold.

  • 59% of reps are imbalanced, and 20 of 33 participants have a mean SI above 0.15. The classes are not equal, but the gap is small.
  • SI ranges from 0 to 0.68. Some participants have a very large difference (Wintana, Afaf and Nora are above 0.5).
  • Among imbalanced reps, the left leg is the weaker one in 68% of cases. A likely reason is that most people are right-leg dominant, but we'd need each participant's dominant leg to confirm it.

# Is the imbalance stable for the same person? Compare set 1 with set 2
per_set = df.groupby(['subject', 'trial']).si_rms.mean().unstack().dropna()
r = np.corrcoef(per_set[1], per_set[2])[0, 1]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.2, 4))
ax.scatter(per_set[1], per_set[2], s=45, color=C_L, edgecolor='white')
ax.plot([0, .65], [0, .65], color=GREY, ls=':')
ax.set_xlabel('mean SI – set 1'); ax.set_ylabel('mean SI – set 2'); ax.set_title(f'Set 1 vs set 2  (r = {r:.2f})')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Figure 6. Mean SI in set 1 vs set 2 for each participant: the imbalance is stable for the same person.

Key finding: SI in the first set is almost the same as in the second (r ≈ 0.96). The imbalance is a stable property of the person, not something that changes randomly from rep to rep, so the label is reliable.

This matters for modeling: a participant's reps look alike. If the same participant's reps end up in both training and testing, the model recognises the person instead of learning imbalance. So in the modeling section we always test on participants the model has never seen.

6. EDA of the features and their relationships¶

This is the main part. We answer six questions:

  1. How does each feature relate to SI?
  2. Do the two legs look alike on each feature?
  3. Which features separate the two classes?
  4. Why are those particular features linked to imbalance?
  5. Which features repeat the same information?
  6. Are the features a property of the person, and do they change with fatigue?

6.1 Correlation of each feature with SI¶

We use Spearman rather than Pearson because it doesn't assume a linear relationship and is less sensitive to outliers. Amplitude features are drawn in one colour, everything else in another.

In [16]:
rho = pd.Series({c: stats.spearmanr(df[c], df.si_rms).correlation for c in FEATURES})
top = rho.reindex(rho.abs().sort_values(ascending=False).index).head(25)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 6.5))
ax.barh(top.index[::-1], top.values[::-1], color=[C_IMB if is_amp(c) else C_L for c in top.index[::-1]], height=.7)
ax.axvline(0, color=GREY, lw=.8); ax.grid(axis='y', visible=False)
ax.set_xlabel('Spearman correlation with SI')
ax.set_title('Top 25 features by correlation with SI\n(purple = amplitude, blue = not amplitude)')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Figure 7. Top 25 features by Spearman correlation with SI. Amplitude features (purple) are the label itself.

What we see:

  • The amplitude features (rms_si, var_si, mav_si, iemg_si) correlate 0.95–1.0 with SI. That's expected, because SI is computed from them. It's also why we can't give them to the model: it would compute the answer directly. That is leakage.
  • wl_si also correlates 0.8, so WL is an amplitude feature even though its name doesn't suggest it.
  • The strongest feature that doesn't depend on amplitude is ssc_rate_si (≈ 0.6), followed by zc_rate_si, env_cv and the frequency differences.

6.2 Do the two legs look alike?¶

For each feature we plot the left leg against the right. Points on the diagonal mean the two legs are similar. Points are coloured by class.

In [17]:
pairs = ['rms', 'ssc_rate', 'mnf', 'mdf', 'env_cv', 'ttp_frac']
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(12, 7.5))
for ax, feat in zip(axes.flat, pairs):
    for lab, col, name in [(0, C_BAL, 'balanced'), (1, C_IMB, 'imbalance')]:
        sub = df[df.label == lab]
        ax.scatter(sub[feat + '_L'], sub[feat + '_R'], s=12, alpha=.6, color=col, label=name)
    lo = min(df[feat + '_L'].min(), df[feat + '_R'].min()); hi = max(df[feat + '_L'].max(), df[feat + '_R'].max())
    ax.plot([lo, hi], [lo, hi], color=GREY, ls=':')
    r = stats.spearmanr(df[feat + '_L'], df[feat + '_R']).correlation
    ax.set_xlabel(feat + ' – left'); ax.set_ylabel(feat + ' – right'); ax.set_title(f'{feat}  (L–R r = {r:.2f})')
axes[0, 0].legend(frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Figure 8. Left leg vs right leg for six features, coloured by class. The diagonal means equal legs.

What we see:

  • For RMS, the purple points (imbalance) sit away from the diagonal and the green ones sit on it. That is the definition of the label.
  • SSC shows the same pattern, but weaker: purple points drift a little further from the diagonal.
  • For frequency (MNF, MDF) and timing (ttp_frac) the two classes overlap. There's a left/right difference for everyone, not only for the imbalanced participants.
  • The left/right correlation for timing is low (~0.4), so the timing of the two legs varies from rep to rep even in balanced participants.

6.3 Features that separate the classes (without amplitude)¶

We rank the amplitude-free features by AUC: how well the feature on its own separates the two classes (0.5 = no separation, 1 = perfect).

In [18]:

    'spearman_SI': [rho[c] for c in NON_AMP],
    'AUC': [max(roc_auc_score(df.label, df[c]), 1 - roc_auc_score(df.label, df[c])) for c in NON_AMP],
}).sort_values('AUC', ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True)
rank.head(12).round(3)

Figure 9. Top 6 amplitude-free features: box plots by class (top) and scatter plots against SI (bottom).

What we see:

  • ssc_rate_si and zc_rate_si: the bigger the left/right difference in how often the signal turns or crosses zero, the higher the SI. In the box plots the imbalance class is clearly higher.
  • env_cv: the envelope of imbalanced participants fluctuates more relative to its mean.
  • But the classes overlap heavily on every feature. No single feature separates them, which already tells us the model's performance will be moderate.

6.4 Why are SSC and ZC linked to imbalance?¶

Our hypothesis: the weaker leg has a weaker signal, so noise makes up a larger share of it. Noise oscillates more, which raises the number of crossings. We check: does the weaker leg (lower RMS) really have a higher SSC?

In [20]:
weak_is_L = df.rms_L < df.rms_R
ssc_weak = np.where(weak_is_L, df.ssc_rate_L, df.ssc_rate_R)
ssc_strong = np.where(weak_is_L, df.ssc_rate_R, df.ssc_rate_L)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.5, 4))
ax.scatter(ssc_strong, ssc_weak, s=12, alpha=.5, color=C_L)
lim = [min(ssc_strong.min(), ssc_weak.min()), max(ssc_strong.max(), ssc_weak.max())]
ax.plot(lim, lim, color=GREY, ls=':')
ax.set_xlabel('SSC rate – stronger leg'); ax.set_ylabel('SSC rate – weaker leg'); ax.set_title('Weaker leg vs stronger leg')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
print(f'Weaker leg has higher SSC in {(ssc_weak > ssc_strong).mean():.0%} of reps')

Weaker leg has higher SSC in 72% of reps

Figure 10. Slope-sign-change rate of the weaker leg vs the stronger leg.

Confirmed: in 72% of reps the weaker leg has the higher SSC. So SSC and ZC see the imbalance indirectly, through the strength of the signal. They're not 100% independent evidence, and the report should say so.

6.5 Features that repeat the same information (redundancy)¶

If two features are very highly correlated, they measure the same thing and one of them is enough.

In [21]:
top15 = rank.feature.head(15).tolist()
corr = df[top15 + ['si_rms']].corr(method='spearman')

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 7))
im = ax.imshow(corr, cmap='RdBu_r', vmin=-1, vmax=1)
ax.set_xticks(range(len(corr)), corr.columns, rotation=90, fontsize=7.5)
ax.set_yticks(range(len(corr)), corr.columns, fontsize=7.5)
ax.grid(False); plt.colorbar(im, fraction=.046); ax.set_title('Correlation between top features and SI')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

C = df[NON_AMP].corr(method='spearman').abs()
redundant = [(a, b, round(C.loc[a, b], 2)) for i, a in enumerate(NON_AMP) for b in NON_AMP[i + 1:] if C.loc[a, b] > 0.9]
pd.DataFrame(redundant, columns=['feature 1', 'feature 2', '|r|']).sort_values('|r|', ascending=False)

feature 1 feature 2 |r|

2 hjorth_mob_R mnf_R 0.98

Figure 11. Correlation heatmap (Spearman) of the top features and SI.

What we see:

  • MNF, Hjorth mobility and spectral entropy are almost the same thing (r = 0.9–0.98). All three measure how fast the signal oscillates. One of them is enough.
  • env_xcorr_peak and env_corr0 are the same thing (0.97).
  • burst_frac and env_kurt are related (0.9): a sharp activation curve means a short active period.
  • ssc_rate_si and zc_rate_si are related, but not to the point of being duplicates.

6.6 Are the features a property of the person? Do they change with fatigue?¶

Property of the person: we split each feature's variation into two parts, between participants and within the same participant. If most of it is between participants, the feature describes the person.

In [22]:
def between_subject_share(col):
    g = df.groupby('subject')[col]
    between, within = g.mean().var(), g.var().mean()
    return between / (between + within)

cols = ['si_rms'] + rank.feature.head(8).tolist() + ['ttp_frac_diff', 'env_corr0']
share = pd.Series({c: between_subject_share(c) for c in cols}).sort_values()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
ax.barh(share.index, share, color=[C_IMB if c == 'si_rms' else C_L for c in share.index], height=.65)
ax.axvline(.5, color=GREY, ls=':'); ax.set_xlim(0, 1); ax.grid(axis='y', visible=False)
ax.set_xlabel('share of variation that is between participants')
ax.set_title('Is the feature a property of the person?')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Figure 12. Share of each feature's variation that lies between participants.

  • 86% of SI's variation is between participants. For the SSC, ZC and MNF differences it's 77–88%, and for env_cv 50–73%. So the strongest features are stable properties of the person, just like SI.
  • Timing (ttp_frac_diff) and coordination (env_corr0) vary mostly within the same participant, from rep to rep. That explains their weak relationship with SI.
In [23]:
# Fatigue: does frequency drop from the first rep to the fifth?
print(df.groupby('rep')[['mdf_L', 'mdf_R']].mean().round(1))
print('SI vs fatigue slope difference (Spearman):', round(rho['mdf_slope_diff'], 3))
print('SI vs rep duration (Spearman):', round(rho['duration_s'], 3))

     mdf_L  mdf_R
rep              
1     64.5   62.4
2     64.3   62.6
3     62.5   62.4
4     62.0   60.0
5     61.1   59.7
SI vs fatigue slope difference (Spearman): -0.016
SI vs rep duration (Spearman): -0.072
  • Median frequency drops about 3 Hz from rep 1 to rep 5 on both legs. That's the classic EMG sign of fatigue.
  • But fatigue is similar in both legs, and the difference in fatigue slope has essentially no relationship with SI. We can't say that the leg that tires faster is the imbalanced one, at least not over just 5 reps.
  • Rep duration has no relationship with SI (≈ −0.07). Slower squatters aren't necessarily imbalanced.

EDA summary¶

Question Answer
Strongest features? The amplitude features, but they are the label itself, so we don't use them
Strongest without amplitude? The left/right SSC difference, then ZC, env_cv and frequency differences
Why SSC? The weaker leg's signal carries more noise, so the link to amplitude is indirect
Any redundancy? MNF ≈ Hjorth mobility ≈ spectral entropy, and env_corr0 ≈ xcorr_peak
Are features a property of the person? The strongest ones are (77–88%), like SI. Timing and coordination are not
Is one leg usually weaker? The left, in 68% of imbalanced reps
Fatigue? Frequency drops 3 Hz, equally in both legs
Does any single feature separate the classes? No, there's heavy overlap, so we expect moderate performance

7. Modeling¶

Feature choice¶

We remove all amplitude features. Section 6.1 showed they correlate 0.8–1.0 with SI, so with them the model would compute the answer directly.

Evaluation: Leave-One-Subject-Out (LOSO)¶

Each fold holds out one whole participant for testing and trains on the rest, 33 times. The reason: a participant's reps look alike (sections 5 and 6.6), and in practice the model will meet new people.

Metrics¶

  • Balanced accuracy instead of plain accuracy, because the classes are not equal.
  • AUC: how well the model separates the two classes.
  • MAE and R² for regression.
In [24]:
from sklearn.model_selection import LeaveOneGroupOut, cross_val_predict
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.dummy import DummyClassifier, DummyRegressor
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression, Ridge
from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier, RandomForestRegressor
from sklearn.metrics import (balanced_accuracy_score, f1_score, confusion_matrix,
                             mean_absolute_error, r2_score)

X = df[NON_AMP]
y_class, y_si, groups = df['label'], df['si_rms'], df['subject']
cv = LeaveOneGroupOut()
print('Features used:', X.shape[1])

Features used: 64

7.1 Classification: is the rep imbalanced?¶

  • Dummy: guesses at random. Any real model has to beat it.
  • Logistic Regression: the simplest model, suited to a small dataset.
  • SVM and Random Forest: more complex, and can pick up non-linear relationships.
In [25]:
classifiers = {
    'Dummy':        DummyClassifier(strategy='stratified', random_state=0),
    'LogReg':       make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(C=0.1, class_weight='balanced', max_iter=5000)),
    'SVM':          make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), SVC(class_weight='balanced', probability=True, random_state=0)),
    'RandomForest': RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, min_samples_leaf=5, class_weight='balanced', random_state=0),
}
class_results, class_probs = [], {}
for name, model in classifiers.items():
    prob = cross_val_predict(model, X, y_class, groups=groups, cv=cv, method='predict_proba')[:, 1]
    class_probs[name] = prob
    class_results.append({'model': name, 'balanced_acc': balanced_accuracy_score(y_class, prob > .5),
                          'F1': f1_score(y_class, prob > .5), 'AUC': roc_auc_score(y_class, prob)})
class_results = pd.DataFrame(class_results).round(3)
class_results

ax.imshow(cm, cmap='Blues'); ax.grid(False)
for i in range(2):
    for j in range(2):
        ax.text(j, i, cm[i, j], ha='center', va='center', fontsize=14, color='white' if cm[i, j] > cm.max() / 2 else 'black')
ax.set_xticks([0, 1], ['balanced', 'imbalance']); ax.set_yticks([0, 1], ['balanced', 'imbalance'])
ax.set_xlabel('predicted'); ax.set_ylabel('true'); ax.set_title('Confusion matrix – LogReg')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Figure 13. Confusion matrix of Logistic Regression (64 features, Leave-One-Subject-Out).

7.2 Regression: predicting the SI value¶

Instead of yes/no we predict the number itself. That carries more information: a participant with SI 0.16 and one with 0.6 are both "imbalance", but they're very different.

  • Dummy: predicts the mean SI for everyone.
  • Ridge: linear regression with regularisation. It produces an equation with one weight per feature.
  • Random Forest: learns rules instead of an equation.
In [27]:
regressors = {
    'Dummy (mean)': DummyRegressor(),
    'Ridge':        make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), Ridge(alpha=10)),
    'RandomForest': RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=300, min_samples_leaf=5, random_state=0),
}
reg_results, reg_preds = [], {}
for name, model in regressors.items():
    pred = cross_val_predict(model, X, y_si, groups=groups, cv=cv)
    reg_preds[name] = pred
    reg_results.append({'model': name, 'MAE': mean_absolute_error(y_si, pred), 'R2': r2_score(y_si, pred)})
reg_results = pd.DataFrame(reg_results).round(3)
reg_results

2 RandomForest 0.094 0.428

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4.2))
for ax, d, title, size in [(axes[0], pd.DataFrame({'true_SI': y_si, 'pred_SI': pred_si}), 'per rep', 18),

Figure 14. Ridge (64 features): true vs predicted SI per rep (left) and per participant (right).

Reading the plot: a perfect model would put every point on the dotted line. The purple lines mark the 0.15 threshold. Most errors are near the threshold: the predicted value is close to the true one but lands on the other side of the line.

7.3 Which features does the model rely on?¶

In [29]:

Figure 15. Ridge weights of the 64-feature model (standardised features).

These are the same features the EDA pointed to. ssc_rate_si has by far the largest weight, followed by env_cv, Hjorth complexity and frequency. The model relies on the relationships we saw in section 6.

7.4 Check: without SSC and ZC¶

Section 6.4 showed that SSC and ZC are indirectly tied to amplitude. We rerun the regression without them to see how much is left.

rows = []
for name in ['Ridge', 'RandomForest']:

    rows.append({'model': name + ' (no ZC/SSC)', 'MAE': mean_absolute_error(y_si, p), 'R2': r2_score(y_si, p)})

7.5 Too many features? (overfitting check)¶

We have 64 features but only 33 participants. With that many features a model can memorise the participants it was trained on instead of learning imbalance. The sign is a big gap between the score on the training data and the score on new participants.

We try keeping only the best k features. The selection (SelectKBest) sits inside the pipeline, so in every LOSO fold it picks the features from the training participants only and never sees the test participant.

In [31]:
from collections import Counter
from sklearn.feature_selection import SelectKBest, f_regression, f_classif
from sklearn.svm import SVR
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsRegressor, KNeighborsClassifier

K_VALUES = [3, 5, 10, 'all']
reg_models = {
    'Ridge':        Ridge(alpha=10),
    'SVR':          SVR(C=1, epsilon=0.02),
    'RandomForest': RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=300, min_samples_leaf=5, random_state=0),
    'kNN':          KNeighborsRegressor(15),
}
clf_models = {
    'LogReg':       LogisticRegression(C=0.1, class_weight='balanced', max_iter=5000),
    'SVM':          SVC(class_weight='balanced', random_state=0),
    'RandomForest': RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, min_samples_leaf=5, class_weight='balanced', random_state=0),
    'kNN':          KNeighborsClassifier(15),
}

def with_k(model, k, score_func):
    return make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), SelectKBest(score_func, k=k), model)

rows = []
for name, model in reg_models.items():
    for k in K_VALUES:
        pipe = with_k(model, k, f_regression)
        test = r2_score(y_si, cross_val_predict(pipe, X, y_si, groups=groups, cv=cv))
        train = r2_score(y_si, pipe.fit(X, y_si).predict(X))
        rows.append({'task': 'regression (R2)', 'model': name, 'k': str(k), 'train': train, 'test': test})
for name, model in clf_models.items():
    for k in K_VALUES:
        pipe = with_k(model, k, f_classif)
        test = balanced_accuracy_score(y_class, cross_val_predict(pipe, X, y_class, groups=groups, cv=cv))
        train = balanced_accuracy_score(y_class, pipe.fit(X, y_class).predict(X))
        rows.append({'task': 'classification (bal. acc)', 'model': name, 'k': str(k), 'train': train, 'test': test})

k_results = pd.DataFrame(rows)
k_results['gap'] = k_results.train - k_results.test
k_results.to_csv('../app/results_feature_count.csv', index=False)   # used by the dashboard
K_COLS = [str(k) for k in K_VALUES]
print('Score on NEW participants (LOSO):')
k_results.pivot_table(index=['task', 'model'], columns='k', values='test')[K_COLS].round(3)

    ax.set_xlabel('number of features'); ax.set_ylabel('score on new participants'); ax.set_title(task)
    ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print('Train minus test (gap). Big gap = overfitting:')
k_results.pivot_table(index=['task', 'model'], columns='k', values='gap')[['3', 'all']].round(2)

Figure 16. Score on new participants vs number of features, for regression (left) and classification (right).

What we see:

  • Fewer features help every model. With all 64 features the flexible models (SVR, Random Forest) score almost perfectly on the training data and much worse on new participants: that's overfitting.
  • With 3–5 features all models end up at roughly the same ceiling (balanced accuracy ≈ 0.65). When a linear model, trees and nearest neighbours all stop at the same place, the limit is the information in the features, not the model.
  • Even with 3 features, Random Forest and SVR still show a large gap. Only the linear models (Ridge, LogReg) have a small gap, because a straight line can't memorise 33 people.

7.6 Final model: Ridge with 3 features¶

Ridge with k = 3 has the best regression score and almost no gap between training and testing. Which features does it pick?

In [33]:
final = with_k(Ridge(alpha=10), 3, f_regression)

picked = Counter()
for train_idx, _ in cv.split(X, y_si, groups):
    selector = final.fit(X.iloc[train_idx], y_si.iloc[train_idx])[1]
    picked.update(X.columns[selector.get_support()])
print('Times each feature was picked (out of 33 folds):', dict(picked))

pred_final = cross_val_predict(final, X, y_si, groups=groups, cv=cv)
per_subj = pd.DataFrame({'subject': groups, 't': y_si, 'p': pred_final}).groupby('subject').mean()
final.fit(X, y_si)
pd.DataFrame({
    'metric': ['MAE', 'R2 per rep', 'R2 per participant', 'R2 on training data',
               'balanced acc (pred SI >= 0.15)', 'AUC'],
    'value': [mean_absolute_error(y_si, pred_final), r2_score(y_si, pred_final), r2_score(per_subj.t, per_subj.p),
              r2_score(y_si, final.predict(X)), balanced_accuracy_score(y_class, pred_final >= SI_THRESHOLD),
              roc_auc_score(y_class, pred_final)],
}).round(3)

The same three features are picked in all 33 folds: zc_rate_si, ssc_rate_si and ssc_rate_diff. These are the features the EDA ranked highest (sections 6.1, 6.3 and 6.4), so the EDA and the model agree. Three features give a better score than 64, with a training score close to the test score, and the model is easy to explain.

7.7 Would more participants help? (learning curve)¶

We train the final model on a growing number of participants and always test on 4 participants it hasn't seen, repeating with random draws. The test set is small, so the R² here is lower than in LOSO. What matters is the shape.

In [35]:
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
subjects = df.subject.unique()
curve = []
for n in [6, 10, 14, 18, 22, 26, 29]:
    scores = []
    for _ in range(100):
        order = rng.permutation(subjects)
        train, test = groups.isin(order[:n]), groups.isin(order[-4:])
        model = with_k(Ridge(alpha=10), 3, f_regression).fit(X[train], y_si[train])
        scores.append(r2_score(y_si[test], model.predict(X[test])))
    curve.append({'participants': n, 'median_R2': np.median(scores)})
curve = pd.DataFrame(curve)
curve.to_csv('../app/results_learning_curve.csv', index=False)   # used by the dashboard

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.3))
ax.plot(curve.participants, curve.median_R2, marker='o', color=C_L)
ax.axhline(0, color=GREY, ls=':')
ax.set_xlabel('participants in training'); ax.set_ylabel('median R2 on 4 new participants')
ax.set_title('Learning curve – Ridge, 3 features'); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
curve.round(3)

Figure 17. Learning curve of the final model (Ridge, 3 features).

The score rises quickly up to about 18 participants and then levels off. More participants alone would probably add little. The bigger limit is the label: SI is computed from amplitude, and amplitude also depends on electrode placement, skin and fat under the skin. Those differences change SI but not the shape or frequency of the signal, so no amplitude-free feature can see them.

9. Insights & conclusion¶

Insights summary¶

Patterns

  • 59% of reps and 20 of 33 participants are imbalanced (SI ≥ 0.15). In 68% of imbalanced reps the left leg is the weaker one.
  • SI is almost the same in set 1 and set 2 (r ≈ 0.96) and 86% of its variation is between participants: imbalance is a property of the person, not of a single rep.
  • Median frequency drops about 3 Hz from rep 1 to rep 5 in both legs (fatigue), equally on both sides.

Interesting relationships

  • The amplitude features (RMS, MAV, VAR, iEMG, WL, envelope) correlate 0.8–1.0 with SI because SI is built from them.
  • Without amplitude, the left/right difference in slope sign changes (ssc_rate_si, ρ 0.61, AUC 0.75) and zero crossings are the strongest. The weaker leg has more slope sign changes in 72% of reps, so this link runs through signal strength (relatively more noise), not an independent cause.
  • MNF, Hjorth mobility and spectral entropy repeat the same information (r 0.90–0.98).
  • Timing and coordination between the legs change from rep to rep and are only weakly related to SI.

Outliers

  • No missing, infinite or duplicate values. SI itself has no IQR outliers, although a few participants have very large SI (Wintana, Afaf, Nora above 0.5). On the SSC/ZC features 6–8% of reps fall outside 1.5 × IQR, and they come from only 3–5 participants (section 4.2). They are real people, not recording errors, so they were kept.
  • Data-quality notes: three participants have only one set, and one set has 4 reps instead of 5.

Key takeaways

  • The classes overlap on every amplitude-free feature, so no single feature separates them.
  • Three features are enough for the best model, and they are the same ones the EDA ranked highest.

Main insights (EDA + model)¶

  • Data and label: 33 participants, 63 sets, 314 reps. The signal is clean; a 20–450 Hz band-pass and a 60 Hz notch are enough. SI is stable between sets, so the label is reliable.
  • Features: amplitude features are the label itself and are excluded. The strongest remaining features are the left/right SSC and ZC differences, then env_cv and the frequency differences.
  • Model: with all 64 features the models overfit (SVR and Random Forest most). Selecting features inside each LOSO fold helps every model, and they reach about the same ceiling. Final model: Ridge with 3 features (zc_rate_si, ssc_rate_si, ssc_rate_diff, picked in all 33 folds): R² ≈ 0.57 on participants it never saw (0.63 per participant), MAE 0.086, with almost no gap to the training score. For yes/no, LogReg with 3 features reaches balanced accuracy ≈ 0.66; Ridge's predicted SI ≥ 0.15 gives 0.62 (AUC 0.72). Most errors sit near the 0.15 threshold.
  • Without SSC/ZC, R² drops to ≈ 0.28 but stays above the baseline, so frequency and signal shape carry real information.

What I learned¶

  • Look at the raw signal and its spectrum before choosing filters, and choose them from the data.
  • Check whether a feature is computed from the label before trusting a high correlation (amplitude here): that is leakage.
  • When the same person appears many times, split by person (Leave-One-Subject-Out); otherwise the model recognises the person instead of the pattern.
  • More features is not better: with 33 people, 3 well-chosen features beat 64, and a train/test gap shows overfitting.
  • A dashboard is only useful when its numbers come from the analysis itself; ours reads the files this notebook writes.

Limitations of the dataset¶

  • Small and specific: 33 participants, all female, 5 reps per set. The learning curve levels off after ~18 participants.
  • The label comes from amplitude, which also depends on electrode placement, skin and fat under the skin. Amplitude-free features cannot see those differences, which caps the model.
  • No motion capture, no maximal voluntary contraction (MVC) and no record of each participant's dominant leg.
  • Sets are short (5 reps), too short to link fatigue to imbalance.

Recommendations for future analysis¶

  • Record an MVC per leg to normalise amplitude before computing SI.
  • Use a label from outside the EMG (a physiotherapist's assessment, a single-leg strength test or a force plate). That would make every feature, amplitude included, a legitimate input.
  • Record each participant's dominant leg, and add more varied participants (men, different training levels).
  • Longer sets, to study whether the weaker leg tires faster.
